analysis.one_liner: Orders EPA to set limits on toxic 'forever chemicals' (PFAS) discharged into water by polluting industries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in May 2022 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, weatherproof clothing, and many industrial processes. The bill directed the EPA to write federal water quality criteria for PFAS and to issue enforceable discharge limits for nine industry categories — chemical and plastics manufacturing, electroplating, metal finishing, textiles, electronics, landfills, leather tanning, paints, and plastics molding — on fixed deadlines between 2024 and 2026, with monitoring required immediately for paper mills and airports. It authorized $12 million for EPA to do the work. The Senate never took it up beyond sending it to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water or eat fish contaminated by industrial PFAS discharges. PFAS do not break down and accumulate in the body; the CRS summary notes they may have adverse human health effects [S2]. Discharge limits would reduce the amount entering rivers, lakes, and drinking-water sources, and immediate monitoring requirements would for the first time tell permit writers which facilities are discharging how much. Communities downstream of chemical plants, textile mills, and landfills would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Directs EPA to publish human health water quality criteria addressing each measurable PFAS chemical or class within three years of enactment [S2][S3].

Requires enforceable discharge limits for nine priority industry categories on fixed deadlines: organic chemicals/plastics/synthetic fibers, electroplating, and metal finishing by June 30, 2024; textile mills, electrical components, and landfills by June 30, 2025; leather tanning, paints, and plastics molding by December 31, 2026 [S3].

Immediately requires monitoring of PFAS discharges — including discharges sent to public sewage treatment plants — for pulp and paper mills and airports, with a deadline for EPA to decide whether to set limits for them by the end of 2027 [S3].
Authorizes $12 million to EPA for implementation in fiscal year 2023 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that discharge PFAS — chemical, plastics, textile, metal-finishing, electronics, paint, leather-tanning makers, and landfill operators — would bear the cost of measuring their discharges and installing treatment to meet new limits. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through prices, and publicly owned sewage treatment plants that receive PFAS-laden industrial waste could face added burdens if industrial users are not fully filtered upstream.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is costly. Installing treatment technology for PFAS at industrial dischargers requires capital investment that would be passed on in product prices, and the bill set fixed statutory deadlines regardless of whether treatment technology is affordable or proven for every category [S3].

The mandate is extremely broad: it requires criteria for 'each measurable' PFAS chemical or class, and the bill's own definition covers any chemical with even one fully fluorinated carbon atom — thousands of substances — on a three-year clock, which critics would call an unworkable pace for a single agency [S3].

Publicly owned treatment works, i.e., local sewer systems, are implicated because the limits cover discharges into them; without commensurate support to those municipal plants, an honest supporter would acknowledge they could absorb costs or legal pressure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit of reducing PFAS at the source is substantial, because these chemicals accumulate in people and water supplies and are expensive to remove once released. The main honest tradeoff is cost to the affected industries and, indirectly, to consumers, plus the strain of Congress mandating deadlines for a very large family of chemicals. The design addresses the largest dischargers first and gives EPA an escape hatch (a reasoned determination) for paper mills and airports where limits may not be feasible [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2022 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never held a markup or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the bill on May 9, 2022; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1][S5].
Four Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS-discharging industries were better off: they faced no new federal discharge limits or monitoring requirements from this bill, and the EPA was left to set PFAS water criteria on its own slower timeline. People exposed to industrial PFAS pollution gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee [S1][S5].

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill after its referral; the bill died in committee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All four cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded in the cosponsor list; the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed enforceable PFAS discharge limits on this category by mid-2024, requiring monitoring and treatment technology. Its interest in avoiding those costs runs against the public interest in uncontaminated water, since untreated PFAS discharges accumulate in drinking water and human bodies [S2][S3].
Facing the earliest 2024 discharge-limit deadline; their savings from discharging untreated PFAS come at the public's expense in contaminated water [S3].
PFAS-based water and stain repellents end up in mill wastewater; the bill would have required limits by 2025 [S3].
Each category would have faced PFAS discharge rules by 2025-2026 under the bill's schedule [S3].

industries.industry: Pulp and paper mills and airports
industries.note: The bill imposed only monitoring — reporting what they discharge — with limits deferred until EPA determined whether they were feasible by 2027, so costs and obligations were lighter than for other categories [S3].
